lines: That bound you just saw decides how long something waits. It says nothing about what that something actually is.
Here's the answer: running totals, buffered rows waiting on a match, anything a query has to remember across triggers.
There are exactly three ways to let that remembered state out.
Hand over only what's brand new since last time. Hand over only what changed. Or hand over the entire thing, every single time, no matter how big it's gotten.
Here's a case worth guessing at before the answer comes.
Take a query that matches two streams against each other as they arrive, and ask it to hand over the entire result every time. Does it run, or does it refuse?
steps.answer: It refuses, flatly. A match between two streams can never take back what it already said.

lines: Refused, and refused immediately, before a single row has even moved.
Not a crash partway through. A flat no, the moment the query is asked to start.
Here's why that particular combination can never work.
Once this kind of query hands over a matched row, it never goes back and revises it. Handing over the entire thing again and again assumes exactly the opposite.
Here's a different case to guess at.
Take that same matching query, and this time give it no sense of how far behind either side is allowed to fall. Does it run, or does it refuse?
steps.answer: It runs fine. What's missing isn't permission -- it's any excuse to ever forget anything.

lines: It runs, and keeps running.
But watch what it's quietly holding onto. Measured directly: the amount it remembers only ever goes up, trigger after trigger, with nothing ever let go.
Here's why it never lets go on its own.
This kind of query keeps a copy of every row from both sides, waiting for its match to show up. Nothing tells it a row has waited long enough to give up on.
Give it that missing piece back, along with a rule for how close in time a match has to be.
Measured: what it remembers climbs for a little while, then holds steady, never climbing past that point again.
Three ways to say what a query hands over, each one ruled in or out by the shape of the query itself.
And a separate rule entirely for what it's allowed to keep remembering in the first place.
